title: A Simple Lesson That Became a Good Lesson
author: Marcus Luther
summary: Marcus Luther, a veteran English teacher in his fifteenth year, walks through a fairly ordinary sophomore lesson to show why it worked and what it reminded him about teaching. He frames the opening weeks as a balancing act between high expectations and care for students, and admits that the balance is tiring. The lesson begins with peer nominations based on the classroom's eight values, moves to a quick better-or-worse anticipation question before Billy Collins' poem "On Turning Ten," and then shifts to a silent gallery walk of classmates' annotations. It ends with individual feedback conferences on a new evidence-and-analysis writing skill. Luther argues that classroom culture and instructional rigor are not a false binary, since rigor that is sustainable depends on culture, and he closes by describing "the right kind of exhausting" as the fatigue of work that feels worthwhile.
points: Starting a lesson with peer nominations and a check-in builds the culture that the later academic work depends on, rather than competing with rigor.
A one-word anticipation question (better or worse after turning ten) exposed a roughly 50/50 split and gave students a reason to read the poem together.
Pivoting mid-lesson to a silent gallery walk of classmates' annotations showed the author trusting students to rise to a challenge, and they did.
Ending with one-on-one feedback conferences, even when the teacher was exhausted, produced coaching and rapport and revealed that students wanted feedback.
Treating exhaustion as either the right kind or the wrong kind helps teachers judge whether their effort goes into choices they believe in.
quotes: I think two things can be true simultaneously: (1) that balancing act matters a great deal for students and (2) that balancing act takes a great deal out of teachers.

The good thing is that this is my second time designing a lesson around this poem, and I am continually reminded as an ELA teacher that the way you help students enter into a new text matters considerably.

30+ students drifting around the room to observe the poems on each other’s desks, poking and prodding at the annotations of their classmates, and then immediately adding more to their own poems when they sit back down.
Too often I see classroom culture and instructional rigor presented as a false binary, as if these are separate paths that lead in opposite directions.

Rather, even though this was my last lesson of the day and I was very much exhausted at this point, I refrained from the temptation of retreating to my desk while they worked independently and instead added one more step:

Each of those individual interactions offered an opportunity, too, for coaching them as writers but also building of invaluable rapport: naming the hard work I had observed from them, thanking them for support of a classmate earlier in a lesson, pointing out an innovative observation that no one else found, or even flipping back to their spiral to show how much of a leap they already had made.
An exhausting in which you feel good about the choices you’re making in your classroom, and also grateful to be able to make the choices you’re making in your classroom.
My mind map takeaway from last week: the teeter-totter between high expectations and care is worth teeter-tottering—even if it’s exhausting.
